newsitem.title: USA: Maine 2-yr budget shortfall seen about $360 mln.
newsitem.headline: Maine 2-yr budget shortfall seen about $360 mln.

text.p: Maine's budget shortfall for its next two-year budget likely will be around $360 million, down about $40 million from early estimates, when Gov. Angus King releases his outline, a state official said on Monday.

"The shortfall seems to be in the vicinity of $360 million," said Keith Todd, deputy state budget officer, explaining King was expected to hold a news conference on Wednesday, when he will disclose some of his plans.

The new budget for the 1998-1999 fiscal years was anticipated to total around $3.7 billion, up slightly from the previous two-year budget, in part due to the elimination of a "tax and match" levy now paid by hospitals.
Ending the tax on hospitals' gross patient revenues, which qualified for federal matching funds, will cost the state about $180 million over the next two budget years, he said.

Some state workers are expected to lose their jobs in the new two-year budget, though the losses are not expected to be as big as in the last pact. "I don't think there's going to be any massive job loss like the current bienium," Todd said.
Rumors that King might propose privatizing the state liquor industry could not be confirmed immediately.

Nor could speculation that the King Administration will recommend repealing or deferring an income tax cap slated to begin with the new 1997 budget, which starts on July 1, and which was projected to cost Maine about $130 million over the next two budget years.
The cap, set at about $676 million of income taxes, would stay in place until income taxes were slashed by 20 percent.
